subject: maths
title: Volume of 3D shapes

slides.heading: Volume — how much space a 3D shape fills
slides.body: Volume measures the three-dimensional space inside a solid shape, so it's always given in cubic units (cm³, m³, mm³). The general rule for any prism is the same: find the area of the cross-section and multiply by the length (or height). A cylinder is a circular prism, so its volume follows exactly the same logic — you just need the area of the circular face first.
slides.note: Maximum 3 sentences. Plain English. No AQA references. What is this and why does it matter.

slides.heading: Volume formulae
slides.formula: Cuboid: V = l × w × h  |  Any prism: V = area of cross-section × length  |  Cylinder: V = πr²h  |  Cone: V = ⅓πr²h  |  Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³  |  Pyramid: V = ⅓ × base area × height
slides.formulaExplained: A cuboid has length l, width w and height h — multiply all three. Any prism (triangular, hexagonal, etc.) has a constant cross-section shape; find that area and multiply by the length the prism extends. A cylinder is a circular prism: the cross-section is a circle with area πr² (r is the radius), and h is the perpendicular height. Cone and pyramid volumes are one-third of the corresponding prism or cylinder with the same base.
slides.whenToUse: Any question about the space inside a 3D solid. Check units — if measurements are in cm, volume is in cm³. Surface area is a different calculation (sum of all face areas).
slides.note: Show formula in standard notation. Explain each variable. State when this formula applies.

slides.heading: Let's work through one
slides.question: A cylinder has a radius of 4 cm and a height of 11 cm. Calculate its volume. Give your answer in terms of π.

steps.instruction: Write the cylinder volume formula and identify r and h.
steps.working: V = πr²h. Here r = 4 cm, h = 11 cm.

slides.conclusion: The volume of the cylinder is 176π cm³ (≈ 552.9 cm³).
slides.note: Numbers must differ from any question in the question bank for this subtopic.

slides.heading: Watch out for this

mistakes.mistake: Using the diameter instead of the radius in V = πr²h — substituting d = 8 when the question gives a diameter of 8 cm.
mistakes.correction: r is always the radius — half the diameter. If the question gives a diameter, halve it before substituting. Double-check by re-reading the question after writing r = ...

mistakes.mistake: Confusing volume (cm³) with surface area (cm²) — calculating the wrong quantity.
mistakes.correction: Volume is how much fits inside — cubic units. Surface area is the total area of all faces — square units. Read the question carefully for the word 'volume' or 'surface area'.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the ⅓ for cones and pyramids — using V = πr²h instead of V = ⅓πr²h.
mistakes.correction: A cone holds exactly one-third the volume of a cylinder with the same base and height. Always include ⅓ for cones and pyramids. These formulae are given on the formula sheet — use it.

slides.note: Minimum 2, maximum 3 mistakes. Specific not generic.

keyFacts.fact: Volume of a cylinder = πr²h. The cross-section is a circle (area = πr²), multiplied by the height h.
keyFacts.examTip: Square the radius before multiplying by π and h — a common error is to write π × r × h, forgetting to square r.

keyFacts.fact: Any prism: V = cross-sectional area × length. Identify the cross-section first, then apply the correct area formula.
keyFacts.examTip: For a triangular prism, find the triangle area (½ × base × height) first, then multiply by the prism's length — don't try to do it in one step.

keyFacts.fact: Cone: V = ⅓πr²h. Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³. Pyramid: V = ⅓ × base area × height. All three are given on the formula sheet.
keyFacts.examTip: Don't memorise cone and sphere formulae under pressure — turn to the formula sheet. But do understand which variable is the radius and which is the height.
